title: Mastering MongoDB Aggregation Pipelines
excerpt: A deep dive into building complex data transformations with MongoDB's aggregation framework — patterns I've learned optimising high-traffic APIs at Justdial.
content:
What Is the Aggregation Pipeline?

The aggregation pipeline in MongoDB is one of the most powerful tools available to any backend developer. Instead of pulling raw documents and processing them in application code, the pipeline lets you run complex transformations, groupings, lookups, and computations directly inside the database — where the data already lives.

At Justdial, I've used aggregations to power dashboards, recommendation feeds, and analytics reports that process millions of documents in under 200ms. Here's everything I've learned.

The Core Stages You Must Know

$match — Filter First, Always

Always put your $match stage as early as possible. It filters documents before any other processing happens, which means MongoDB can use indexes and avoid scanning the entire collection.

// ❌ Slow — processes all docs then filters
[
  { $group: { _id: "$city", total: { $sum: 1 } } },
  { $match: { total: { $gt: 100 } } }
]

// ✅ Fast — filters early, uses index
[
  { $match: { city: "Mumbai", createdAt: { $gte: ISODate("2024-01-01") } } },
  { $group: { _id: "$city", total: { $sum: 1 } } }
]

$group — Aggregating Documents

The $group stage collapses multiple documents into a single result. Think of it as MongoDB's version of SQL's GROUP BY.

// Count orders per user, sum their total spend
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "completed" } },
  {
    $group: {
      _id: "$userId",
      orderCount: { $sum: 1 },
      totalSpend: { $sum: "$amount" },
      avgOrderValue: { $avg: "$amount" },
      firstOrder: { $min: "$createdAt" },
      lastOrder: { $max: "$createdAt" }
    }
  },
  { $sort: { totalSpend: -1 } },
  { $limit: 10 }
])

$lookup — Joining Collections

MongoDB isn't a relational database, but $lookup lets you perform SQL-style JOIN operations between collections. Use it carefully — it's powerful but expensive at scale.

// Join orders with users
db.orders.aggregate([
  {
    $lookup: {
      from: "users",
      localField: "userId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "user"
    }
  },
  { $unwind: "$user" },
  {
    $project: {
      orderId: 1,
      amount: 1,
      "user.name": 1,
      "user.email": 1
    }
  }
])

$facet — Multiple Pipelines in One Query

This is my favourite underused stage. $facet runs multiple sub-pipelines on the same input simultaneously and returns all results in a single query — perfect for paginated APIs that need both data and count.

db.products.aggregate([
  { $match: { category: "electronics" } },
  {
    $facet: {
      data: [
        { $sort: { price: 1 } },
        { $skip: 0 },
        { $limit: 20 }
      ],
      totalCount: [
        { $count: "count" }
      ],
      priceStats: [
        {
          $group: {
            _id: null,
            min: { $min: "$price" },
            max: { $max: "$price" },
            avg: { $avg: "$price" }
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
])

Performance Optimisation Tips

  • Index your $match fields. Create compound indexes that match the shape of your queries. explain("executionStats") is your best friend.
  • Avoid $unwind on large arrays without a preceding $match. It multiplies your document count.
  • Use $project to drop fields early. The fewer fields flowing through the pipeline, the less memory consumed.
  • allowDiskUse: true for pipelines that might exceed 100MB RAM limit in production.
  • Avoid $where and $function — they run JavaScript in the DB process and bypass query optimiser.

Real-World Pattern: Leaderboard Query

// Top 10 users by engagement score this month
db.activities.aggregate([
  {
    $match: {
      createdAt: {
        $gte: new Date(new Date().getFullYear(), new Date().getMonth(), 1)
      }
    }
  },
  {
    $group: {
      _id: "$userId",
      posts: { $sum: { $cond: [{ $eq: ["$type", "post"] }, 1, 0] } },
      comments: { $sum: { $cond: [{ $eq: ["$type", "comment"] }, 1, 0] } },
      likes: { $sum: { $cond: [{ $eq: ["$type", "like"] }, 1, 0] } }
    }
  },
  {
    $addFields: {
      score: {
        $add: [
          { $multiply: ["$posts", 10] },
          { $multiply: ["$comments", 3] },
          "$likes"
        ]
      }
    }
  },
  { $sort: { score: -1 } },
  { $limit: 10 },
  {
    $lookup: {
      from: "users",
      localField: "_id",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "userInfo"
    }
  },
  { $unwind: "$userInfo" }
])

Closing Thoughts

The aggregation pipeline is what separates a MongoDB beginner from an expert. Once you understand how to push computation into the database layer, you'll find yourself writing faster, cleaner, and more scalable APIs. Always profile with explain() and index strategically — the pipeline is only as fast as your indexes allow.
author: Owais Rafiq

title: Next.js App Router: Everything You Need to Know
excerpt: A practical guide to migrating from Pages Router to App Router — Server Components, streaming, and the mental model shift that makes it click.
content:
Why the App Router Exists

The Pages Router was Next.js's original architecture — every file in /pages became a route, and everything ran either on the server (via getServerSideProps) or client side. It worked well, but it had limits: you couldn't colocate components with routes, data fetching patterns were rigid, and React's new concurrent features were hard to leverage.

The App Router, introduced in Next.js 13 and stabilised in 14, is a ground-up redesign built on React Server Components. It changes how you think about the server/client boundary.

The Core Mental Model: Server by Default

The single most important thing to understand: every component in the App Router is a Server Component by default. They run on the server, generate HTML, and send zero JavaScript to the browser unless you explicitly opt into the client.

// app/page.tsx — This runs on the SERVER only
// No useEffect, no useState, no browser APIs
import { db } from '@/lib/db'

export default async function HomePage() {
  const posts = await db.posts.findMany() // Direct DB call!
  
  return (
    

      {posts.map(post => (
        

          
{post.title}

        

      ))}
    

  )
}

The big win: you can await data directly inside components without getServerSideProps. No prop drilling, no API routes for internal data fetching.

Client Components — Opt In With "use client"

When you need interactivity, state, or browser APIs, add "use client" at the top of the file. This creates a boundary — everything below that file runs on the client.

"use client" // ← This one directive changes everything

import { useState } from 'react'

export function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
  
  return (
    
  )
}
Key insight: Server Components CAN render Client Components as children, but Client Components CANNOT render Server Components. Push "use client" as deep into the tree as possible.

The File System Conventions

app/
├── layout.tsx          ← Persistent shell (nav, footer)
├── page.tsx            ← / route
├── loading.tsx         ← Suspense fallback
├── error.tsx           ← Error boundary
├── not-found.tsx       ← 404 page
├── blog/
│   ├── page.tsx        ← /blog
│   └── [slug]/
│       └── page.tsx    ← /blog/:slug
└── (marketing)/        ← Route group (no URL segment)
    └── about/
        └── page.tsx    ← /about

Data Fetching Patterns

Static Generation (Default)

// Runs at BUILD TIME — generates static HTML
export default async function BlogPost({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }) {
  const post = await getPost(params.slug)
  return 
{post.content}

}

// Tell Next.js all possible slugs at build time
export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const posts = await getAllPosts()
  return posts.map(post => ({ slug: post.slug }))
}

Dynamic (SSR) — opt in with cache: 'no-store'

async function getData() {
  const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data', {
    cache: 'no-store' // Runs on every request
  })
  return res.json()
}

Revalidation — the best of both worlds

const data = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products', {
  next: { revalidate: 3600 } // Re-fetch every 1 hour (ISR)
})

Streaming with Suspense

App Router supports React Suspense natively. Wrap slow components in <Suspense> to stream the page progressively — fast content shows immediately while slow data loads in the background.

import { Suspense } from 'react'
import { Skeleton } from '@/components/ui/Skeleton'

export default function Dashboard() {
  return (
    

      
Dashboard
  {/* Shows immediately */}
      
      }>
          {/* Streams in when ready */}
      
    

  )
}

Migration Tips from Pages Router

  • Move _app.tsx logic into app/layout.tsx
  • Replace getServerSideProps with async component + direct data fetching
  • Replace getStaticPaths + getStaticProps with generateStaticParams
  • Replace useRouter().query with the params / searchParams props
  • Move API routes to app/api/route.ts using the new Route Handlers

Is It Worth Migrating?

Yes, but don't rush it. For new projects, absolutely use App Router from day one. For existing projects, migrate incrementally — the Pages and App Routers can coexist in the same project during migration. The productivity gain and performance improvement for data-heavy apps is significant.
author: Owais Rafiq

title: Node.js Performance Optimization: 10 Battle-Tested Techniques
excerpt: Real techniques I've used to take Node.js APIs from 500ms to under 50ms response times — covering async patterns, clustering, caching, and database query tuning.
content:
Why Node.js Performance Matters

Node.js is single-threaded. That's both its superpower and its Achilles heel. Done right, it handles thousands of concurrent connections efficiently. Done wrong, one blocking operation starves every request in the queue. These are the 10 most impactful optimisations I've applied in production systems.

1. Never Block the Event Loop

The event loop is Node's heartbeat. Any synchronous CPU-heavy work blocks it entirely. Use setImmediate() or worker threads for heavy computation.

// ❌ Blocks the event loop for ALL requests
app.get('/process', (req, res) => {
  const result = heavyCPUWork(req.body.data) // blocks!
  res.json(result)
})

// ✅ Offload to Worker Thread
import { Worker } from 'worker_threads'

app.get('/process', async (req, res) => {
  const result = await runInWorker('./worker.js', req.body.data)
  res.json(result)
})

2. Use Clustering to Utilise All CPU Cores

Node runs on a single core by default. On a 16-core machine, you're wasting 93% of your CPU. Use the cluster module to spawn one worker per core.

import cluster from 'cluster'
import os from 'os'

if (cluster.isPrimary) {
  const cpuCount = os.cpus().length
  console.log(`Spawning ${cpuCount} workers`)
  
  for (let i = 0; i < cpuCount; i++) {
    cluster.fork()
  }
  
  cluster.on('exit', (worker) => {
    console.log(`Worker ${worker.process.pid} died. Restarting...`)
    cluster.fork() // Auto-restart crashed workers
  })
} else {
  // Each worker runs your Express app
  import('./app').then(({ app }) => app.listen(3000))
}

3. Cache Aggressively with Redis

The fastest database query is the one you never make. Cache hot data in Redis and serve it from memory.

import Redis from 'ioredis'
const redis = new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL)

async function getCachedUser(userId: string) {
  const cacheKey = `user:${userId}`
  
  // Try cache first
  const cached = await redis.get(cacheKey)
  if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached)
  
  // Cache miss — fetch from DB
  const user = await User.findById(userId)
  if (!user) return null
  
  // Cache for 15 minutes
  await redis.setex(cacheKey, 900, JSON.stringify(user))
  return user
}

4. Use Connection Pooling for Databases

Creating a new database connection on every request is expensive. Use a connection pool and reuse existing connections.

// Mongoose connection pool (default: 5)
mongoose.connect(process.env.MONGO_URI, {
  maxPoolSize: 20,     // Max concurrent connections
  minPoolSize: 5,      // Keep 5 connections ready
  socketTimeoutMS: 30000,
  serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 5000
})

// MySQL with mysql2 pool
const pool = mysql.createPool({
  host: process.env.DB_HOST,
  user: process.env.DB_USER,
  database: process.env.DB_NAME,
  connectionLimit: 20,  // Pool size
  queueLimit: 0
})

// Always use pool.promise().query() not individual connections

5. Avoid Async/Await Waterfalls

Sequential awaits are a silent performance killer. Run independent async operations in parallel.

// ❌ Sequential — 300ms total (100 + 100 + 100)
const user = await getUser(id)
const orders = await getOrders(id)
const notifications = await getNotifications(id)

// ✅ Parallel — 100ms total (all run concurrently)
const [user, orders, notifications] = await Promise.all([
  getUser(id),
  getOrders(id),
  getNotifications(id)
])

6. Stream Large Responses

Don't buffer an entire 100MB file in memory before sending. Stream it directly to the client.

import { createReadStream } from 'fs'

app.get('/download/:file', (req, res) => {
  const filePath = path.join(__dirname, 'files', req.params.file)
  
  res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/octet-stream')
  
  // Stream — never loads entire file into memory
  createReadStream(filePath).pipe(res)
})

7. Compress HTTP Responses

import compression from 'compression'

app.use(compression({
  level: 6,      // Compression level (1-9)
  threshold: 1024 // Only compress responses > 1KB
}))

// Typical savings: 60-70% on JSON responses

8. Use Pagination — Never Return All Records

// ❌ Returns potentially millions of records
app.get('/users', async (req, res) => {
  const users = await User.find({})
  res.json(users)
})

// ✅ Cursor-based pagination (better than offset for large sets)
app.get('/users', async (req, res) => {
  const { cursor, limit = 20 } = req.query
  
  const query = cursor ? { _id: { $gt: cursor } } : {}
  
  const users = await User.find(query)
    .sort({ _id: 1 })
    .limit(Number(limit) + 1) // +1 to check if there's a next page
    .lean() // Returns plain objects, not Mongoose documents
  
  const hasMore = users.length > limit
  if (hasMore) users.pop()
  
  res.json({
    data: users,
    nextCursor: hasMore ? users[users.length - 1]._id : null
  })
})

9. Add Database Indexes Strategically

// Always index fields you query/sort on
const UserSchema = new Schema({
  email: { type: String, index: true, unique: true }, // Query by email
  createdAt: { type: Date, index: true },             // Sort by date
  
  // Compound index for common query pattern
  // db.users.find({ city, status }).sort({ createdAt })
})

UserSchema.index({ city: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 })

// Check your indexes regularly
// db.collection.getIndexes()
// db.collection.find().explain('executionStats')

10. Monitor with APM Tools

You can't optimise what you can't measure. Add New Relic, Datadog, or even the built-in --prof V8 profiler to find real bottlenecks before guessing.

// Quick profiling with clinic.js
// npm install -g clinic
clinic doctor -- node server.js
clinic flame -- node server.js
clinic bubbleprof -- node server.js

Summary

Start with the lowest-hanging fruit: parallel async operations and Redis caching usually give the biggest wins for the least effort. Then add connection pooling and clustering. Measure before and after every change — in production, intuition is unreliable. Let the profiler guide you.
author: Owais Rafiq

title: React Best Practices 2024 — Write Code Your Future Self Will Thank You For
excerpt: The patterns and practices that separate maintainable React applications from ones that become nightmares six months later — from state management to component design.
content:
React Has Grown Up — Have Your Patterns?

React in 2024 is fundamentally different from React in 2019. Hooks replaced class components, Server Components changed the data model, and concurrent features rewired how we think about rendering. But many codebases still carry old patterns that made sense in 2019 and cause pain today. Here's how to write React that ages well.

1. Co-locate State as Low as Possible

The most common React performance problem isn't caused by slow rendering — it's caused by state living too high in the tree, triggering re-renders in components that don't need them.

// ❌ State at root causes entire tree to re-render on every keystroke
function App() {
  const [searchQuery, setSearchQuery] = useState('')
  
  return (
    

        {/* Re-renders on every keystroke! */}
      
      
    

  )
}

// ✅ Encapsulate state in the component that needs it
function SearchSection() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('')
  return (
    

      
      
    

  )
}

function App() {
  return (
    

        {/* Never re-renders from search state */}
      
    

  )
}

2. Custom Hooks for Business Logic

If your component has more than 3-4 useState/useEffect calls, extract them into a custom hook. Components should describe UI — hooks should describe behaviour.

// ❌ Logic mixed into component
function UserProfile({ userId }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null)
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true)
  const [error, setError] = useState(null)
  
  useEffect(() => {
    setLoading(true)
    fetchUser(userId)
      .then(setUser)
      .catch(setError)
      .finally(() => setLoading(false))
  }, [userId])
  
  if (loading) return 
  if (error) return 
  return 
{user.name}

}

// ✅ Extract into a reusable hook
function useUser(userId) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null)
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true)
  const [error, setError] = useState(null)
  
  useEffect(() => {
    setLoading(true)
    fetchUser(userId)
      .then(setUser)
      .catch(setError)
      .finally(() => setLoading(false))
  }, [userId])
  
  return { user, loading, error }
}

function UserProfile({ userId }) {
  const { user, loading, error } = useUser(userId)
  
  if (loading) return 
  if (error) return 
  return 
{user.name}

}

3. useCallback and useMemo — Use Them Right

These hooks exist to prevent unnecessary re-renders and recomputations. The mistake is using them everywhere. The rule: only memoize when you have a measured performance problem.

// useMemo — only for expensive calculations
const sortedAndFilteredList = useMemo(() => {
  return largeDataset
    .filter(item => item.active)
    .sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name))
}, [largeDataset]) // Recalculates only when largeDataset changes

// useCallback — only when passing callbacks to memoized children
const handleSubmit = useCallback((data) => {
  // prevent creating a new function reference on every render
  onSubmit(data)
}, [onSubmit])

4. Error Boundaries Are Not Optional

In production, components will crash. Without error boundaries, one broken component crashes the entire app. Wrap major UI sections in error boundaries to isolate failures.

"use client" // Error boundaries must be client components

import { Component, type ReactNode } from 'react'

class ErrorBoundary extends Component<
  { children: ReactNode; fallback: ReactNode },
  { hasError: boolean }
> {
  state = { hasError: false }
  
  static getDerivedStateFromError() {
    return { hasError: true }
  }
  
  render() {
    if (this.state.hasError) return this.props.fallback
    return this.props.children
  }
}

// Usage
Something went wrong in this section.}>

5. Compound Components for Flexible APIs

Instead of a single component with 20 props, the compound component pattern gives consumers full control over layout and behaviour while keeping logic centralised.

// ❌ Prop explosion
Read}
  headerStyle="large"
/>

// ✅ Compound components — composable, readable

  
    
  
  
    Post
    Author

6. Avoid useEffect for Derived State

// ❌ Common mistake — unnecessary useEffect
const [items, setItems] = useState([])
const [filteredItems, setFilteredItems] = useState([])

useEffect(() => {
  setFilteredItems(items.filter(item => item.active))
}, [items])

// ✅ Compute during render — simpler, no timing issues
const [items, setItems] = useState([])
const filteredItems = items.filter(item => item.active)

7. TypeScript: Type Your Props Properly

// ❌ Vague typing
interface ButtonProps {
  onClick: Function
  children: any
  style?: object
}

// ✅ Precise typing
interface ButtonProps {
  onClick: (event: React.MouseEvent) => void
  children: React.ReactNode
  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'ghost'
  size?: 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg'
  disabled?: boolean
  loading?: boolean
  className?: string
}

Final Thoughts

Good React code isn't about using the most advanced patterns — it's about being intentional. Co-locate state, extract logic into hooks, type everything, and add error boundaries. These four habits alone will make your codebase significantly easier to maintain and extend. The rest follows naturally.
author: Owais Rafiq

title: AI Integration for Developers: A Practical Guide to Building with LLMs
excerpt: Stop waiting for AI to change your industry — start building with it today. A developer's practical guide to integrating LLMs into real applications with the Anthropic and OpenAI APIs.
content:
AI Is Now a Standard Library

In 2024, integrating AI into your application is as straightforward as integrating a payment gateway or a mapping API. The barriers are low, the APIs are clean, and the use cases are practically limitless. Here's a practical guide to actually shipping AI features, not just experimenting with them in notebooks.

Understanding LLM Basics for Developers

A Large Language Model (LLM) is a text-in, text-out function. You send a prompt, it returns a response. The magic is in its emergent understanding of language, code, and reasoning. For developers, think of it as an API call that returns intelligently generated text.

  • Context window: how many tokens the model can process at once (GPT-4: 128k, Claude: 200k)
  • Temperature: controls randomness. 0 = deterministic, 1 = creative. Use 0 for code, 0.7 for writing
  • System prompt: instructions that define the model's role and behaviour
  • Tokens: roughly 1 token ≈ 0.75 words in English

Getting Started: Your First LLM API Call

import Anthropic from '@anthropic-ai/sdk'

const client = new Anthropic({ apiKey: process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY })

async function summariseText(text: string): Promise {
  const message = await client.messages.create({
    model: 'claude-opus-4-8',
    max_tokens: 1024,
    system: 'You are a helpful assistant. Summarise text clearly and concisely.',
    messages: [
      {
        role: 'user',
        content: `Please summarise the following text:\n\n${text}`
      }
    ]
  })
  
  return message.content[0].type === 'text' ? message.content[0].text : ''
}

// Usage
const summary = await summariseText(longArticle)

Building a Practical Feature: AI Code Review

Here's how to build an AI code reviewer that integrates into your workflow:

import Anthropic from '@anthropic-ai/sdk'

const client = new Anthropic()

async function reviewCode(code: string, language: string) {
  const stream = await client.messages.stream({
    model: 'claude-opus-4-8',
    max_tokens: 2048,
    system: `You are an expert ${language} code reviewer. 
    Review the code for: bugs, security issues, performance problems, 
    and style improvements. Be specific and actionable.`,
    messages: [
      {
        role: 'user',
        content: `Review this ${language} code:\n\n\`\`\`${language}\n${code}\n\`\`\``
      }
    ]
  })
  
  // Stream the response token by token
  for await (const chunk of stream) {
    if (chunk.type === 'content_block_delta') {
      process.stdout.write(chunk.delta.text)
    }
  }
}

await reviewCode(myNodeJsCode, 'javascript')

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

LLMs have a knowledge cutoff. For domain-specific knowledge (your product docs, codebase, company data), use RAG: embed your data, retrieve relevant chunks, and include them in the prompt as context.

// Simplified RAG pattern
async function answerWithContext(question: string, docs: string[]) {
  // 1. Retrieve relevant documents (via vector similarity search)
  const relevantDocs = await vectorDB.search(question, { topK: 5 })
  
  // 2. Build context from retrieved docs
  const context = relevantDocs
    .map((doc, i) => `[Source ${i+1}]: ${doc.content}`)
    .join('\n\n')
  
  // 3. Include context in prompt
  const response = await client.messages.create({
    model: 'claude-opus-4-8',
    max_tokens: 1024,
    messages: [{
      role: 'user',
      content: `Answer the question using only the provided context.

Context:
${context}

Question: ${question}`
    }]
  })
  
  return response.content[0].text
}

Tool Use / Function Calling

Modern LLMs can call functions you define. This is how you build AI agents that actually do things, not just talk about them.

const tools = [
  {
    name: 'get_weather',
    description: 'Get the current weather for a city',
    input_schema: {
      type: 'object',
      properties: {
        city: { type: 'string', description: 'City name' }
      },
      required: ['city']
    }
  }
]

const response = await client.messages.create({
  model: 'claude-opus-4-8',
  max_tokens: 1024,
  tools,
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'What is the weather in Srinagar?' }]
})

// If model wants to call a tool
if (response.stop_reason === 'tool_use') {
  const toolCall = response.content.find(c => c.type === 'tool_use')
  const weatherData = await getWeather(toolCall.input.city)
  // Send result back to model to continue
}

Rate Limiting and Cost Management

  • Cache responses for identical prompts using Redis with a TTL
  • Set hard max_tokens limits — runaway prompts can get expensive
  • Use smaller models (Claude Haiku, GPT-3.5) for simple classification tasks
  • Batch similar requests when possible
  • Monitor token usage and set alerts on your API dashboard

What to Build First

The most impactful AI features for most applications: semantic search (better than keyword search), automatic summarisation (long content made scannable), smart form filling (auto-populate from unstructured input), and code generation assistance (internal tooling). Start small, measure the impact, then expand.
author: Owais Rafiq

title: MySQL vs MongoDB: Choosing the Right Database for Your Project
excerpt: Both MySQL and MongoDB are excellent databases — but they solve different problems. Here's a practical breakdown of when to use each, with real examples and query comparisons.
content:
The Question You Should Actually Be Asking

The MySQL vs MongoDB debate is often framed as SQL vs NoSQL, relational vs document. But the real question is simpler: what shape is your data, and how do you need to query it? Both databases are mature, battle-tested, and capable of running in production at enormous scale. The choice depends on your use case, not tribal loyalty.

MySQL: When to Choose It

MySQL (and relational databases generally) shine when:

  • Your data has clear relationships between entities (users → orders → products)
  • You need ACID transactions across multiple tables
  • Your schema is well-defined and unlikely to change frequently
  • You're doing complex analytical queries with multiple JOINs
  • You have strict data integrity requirements
-- MySQL: Find top customers by revenue with their order counts
SELECT 
  u.id,
  u.name,
  u.email,
  COUNT(o.id) AS order_count,
  SUM(o.total_amount) AS total_revenue
FROM users u
INNER JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  AND o.created_at >= DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 30 DAY)
GROUP BY u.id, u.name, u.email
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
LIMIT 10;

MongoDB: When to Choose It

MongoDB excels when:

  • Your data is hierarchical or document-like (user profile with nested address, preferences, history)
  • The schema evolves rapidly during early development
  • You're storing unstructured or semi-structured data
  • You need horizontal scaling across multiple servers
  • You're building real-time applications with flexible data shapes
// MongoDB: Store a rich user profile as one document
// No JOINs needed — data you access together is stored together
db.users.insertOne({
  _id: ObjectId(),
  name: "Owais Rafiq",
  email: "owais@example.com",
  address: {
    city: "Srinagar",
    state: "J&K",
    country: "India"
  },
  skills: ["Node.js", "React", "MongoDB"],
  preferences: {
    theme: "dark",
    notifications: { email: true, push: false }
  },
  createdAt: new Date()
})

Query Comparison: Same Task, Both Databases

Finding active users in a specific city

-- MySQL
SELECT id, name, email 
FROM users 
WHERE city = 'Mumbai' 
  AND status = 'active' 
  AND last_login > DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 7 DAY);

// MongoDB
db.users.find({
  "address.city": "Mumbai",
  status: "active",
  lastLogin: { $gt: new Date(Date.now() - 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000) }
})

Transactions: MySQL has the Edge

-- MySQL transactions are rock-solid
START TRANSACTION;

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2;
INSERT INTO transactions (from_id, to_id, amount) VALUES (1, 2, 500);

COMMIT; -- All or nothing. If anything fails, nothing happens

// MongoDB also supports transactions (v4.0+) but with overhead
const session = client.startSession()
try {
  session.startTransaction()
  await Account.updateOne({ _id: 1 }, { $inc: { balance: -500 } }, { session })
  await Account.updateOne({ _id: 2 }, { $inc: { balance: 500 } }, { session })
  await session.commitTransaction()
} catch (error) {
  await session.abortTransaction()
} finally {
  session.endSession()
}

Performance at Scale

MySQL scales vertically well and horizontally through read replicas. For write-heavy workloads at massive scale, it requires sharding which adds operational complexity.

MongoDB was designed with horizontal scaling in mind. Its built-in sharding and replica sets make it easier to distribute data across multiple servers. This is why it's popular for applications with unpredictable growth patterns.

The Hybrid Approach

Many production systems use both. A common pattern:

  • MySQL: Financial data, user accounts, orders — anything requiring strict consistency and complex relational queries
  • MongoDB: Product catalogue, user activity feeds, logs, content — anything document-like or schema-flexible
  • Redis: Session data, caching, real-time counters

My Recommendation

Default to MySQL/PostgreSQL when in doubt. Relational databases have decades of tooling, documentation, and proven operational practices. Move to MongoDB when you have a clear, specific need: schema flexibility, document-oriented data, or horizontal scaling requirements you've already hit. Using MongoDB for everything "because it's modern" is a mistake many teams have regretted.
author: Owais Rafiq

title: Python for Backend Developers: FastAPI, Async, and Building Modern APIs
excerpt: Python is no longer just for data science. FastAPI and async Python have made it a serious choice for building high-performance backend APIs — here's how to get started.
content:
Python's Backend Renaissance

Python has always been popular, but for backend web APIs, it was often seen as slow and better suited to data science or scripting. That changed with the introduction of async Python (asyncio) and FastAPI — a modern framework that rivals Node.js in performance while providing automatic API documentation and full type safety.

Why FastAPI?

FastAPI is built on top of Starlette (ASGI framework) and Pydantic (data validation). Its key advantages:

  • One of the fastest Python frameworks available (only Starlette and Uvicorn are faster)
  • Automatic OpenAPI/Swagger documentation generated from your code
  • Full type safety with Python type hints
  • Native async/await support
  • Dependency injection built in

Building Your First FastAPI Application

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Depends
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr
from typing import Optional
import motor.motor_asyncio  # Async MongoDB driver

app = FastAPI(title="My API", version="1.0.0")

# Pydantic models for request/response validation
class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: EmailStr
    age: Optional[int] = None

class UserResponse(BaseModel):
    id: str
    name: str
    email: str

# MongoDB connection
client = motor.motor_asyncio.AsyncIOMotorClient("mongodb://localhost:27017")
db = client.myapp

@app.post("/users", response_model=UserResponse, status_code=201)
async def create_user(user: UserCreate):
    # FastAPI auto-validates the request body against UserCreate
    user_dict = user.dict()
    result = await db.users.insert_one(user_dict)
    user_dict["id"] = str(result.inserted_id)
    return user_dict

@app.get("/users/{user_id}", response_model=UserResponse)
async def get_user(user_id: str):
    user = await db.users.find_one({"_id": ObjectId(user_id)})
    if not user:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="User not found")
    user["id"] = str(user["_id"])
    return user

Async Python: How It Works

Python's asyncio is similar to Node.js's event loop — it enables concurrency without threads by yielding control during I/O operations.

import asyncio
import httpx  # Async HTTP client

async def fetch_data(url: str):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        response = await client.get(url)
        return response.json()

async def main():
    # Sequential — slow (runs one after another)
    data1 = await fetch_data("https://api1.example.com/data")
    data2 = await fetch_data("https://api2.example.com/data")
    
    # Concurrent — fast (runs simultaneously)
    data1, data2 = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch_data("https://api1.example.com/data"),
        fetch_data("https://api2.example.com/data")
    )

Dependency Injection in FastAPI

FastAPI's dependency injection system is elegant. Use it for authentication, database sessions, and shared configuration.

from fastapi import Depends, Security
from fastapi.security import HTTPBearer
import jwt

security = HTTPBearer()

async def get_current_user(token = Security(security)):
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token.credentials, SECRET_KEY, algorithms=["HS256"])
        user = await db.users.find_one({"_id": payload["sub"]})
        if not user:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="User not found")
        return user
    except jwt.ExpiredSignatureError:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Token expired")

# Use the dependency on any route
@app.get("/profile")
async def get_profile(current_user = Depends(get_current_user)):
    return current_user

Python vs Node.js: When to Use Each

  • Choose Python/FastAPI when: your team knows Python, you need ML model serving, heavy data processing, or rich scientific libraries
  • Choose Node.js when: building real-time apps (WebSockets), your team is JavaScript-heavy, or you want one language across frontend and backend
  • Performance: Both are competitive for I/O bound workloads. Node.js edges out for real-time; Python edges out when ML is involved

Running FastAPI in Production

# Install dependencies
pip install fastapi uvicorn gunicorn

# Development server
uvicorn main:app --reload

# Production: Gunicorn managing multiple Uvicorn workers
gunicorn main:app \
  -w 4 \
  -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker \
  --bind 0.0.0.0:8000

# Or with Docker
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["gunicorn", "main:app", "-w", "4", "-k", "uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker"]

Final Thoughts

FastAPI has genuinely changed Python's position in backend development. If you're a JavaScript developer curious about Python, or a data scientist who wants to productionise their models as APIs, FastAPI is the right entry point. The async model is familiar, the documentation is outstanding, and the type safety makes large codebases maintainable. Give it a week — you'll be surprised how productive you become.
author: Owais Rafiq

title: From Kashmir to Software Engineering
excerpt: My journey from a computer science student in Srinagar to working as a backend engineer at one of India's largest tech companies — what I learned along the way.
content:
Where It Started

I grew up in Srinagar, Kashmir — a city more famous for its mountains and Mughal gardens than its tech scene. When I started studying Computer Science, I had no senior developers around me to mentor me, no local tech meetups, and spotty internet connectivity that made downloading tutorials a genuine challenge.

What I did have was curiosity, time, and the realisation that the internet had already democratised access to world-class education. A student in Kashmir could learn from the same YouTube channels, documentation, and open-source projects as someone in Silicon Valley. That realisation changed everything.

The Early Days: HTML and Copying Code

I started with HTML and CSS, like most developers of my generation. I would copy-paste code from tutorials, change a colour here, a font there, and feel the disproportionate satisfaction of seeing something change on screen. That feedback loop — make a change, see a result immediately — is what makes web development uniquely addictive.

My first "real" project was a personal website. It looked terrible. The gradient was too aggressive, the fonts were mismatched, and it only worked on one browser. But it was mine, deployed on GitHub Pages, accessible to anyone in the world with a URL. That felt like magic.

JavaScript: The Language That Changed Everything

When I discovered JavaScript could make pages interactive, I fell down a rabbit hole I've never climbed out of. I built Simon's Game, a Drum Kit, a Shooting Game — tiny projects that most people would dismiss but each one taught me something fundamental: event listeners, async code, DOM manipulation, the concept of state.

The best way to learn programming is to build things you actually want to use, even if those things are small and silly.

Node.js was the turning point. Suddenly, JavaScript wasn't just for making buttons animate — it could power databases, handle HTTP requests, process files, and serve millions of users. I spent months reading every tutorial I could find, building REST APIs from scratch, breaking them, rebuilding them better.

Getting Hired at Justdial

The interview process at Justdial was the most rigorous evaluation I'd ever faced. Data structures, system design, Node.js internals, database optimisation — they tested everything. I failed my first attempt at a similar company and spent three months filling the gaps before trying again.

Preparation tips that actually worked for me:

  • Build something substantial — a full-stack project you can speak about for 20 minutes
  • Read Node.js documentation, not just tutorials. Understand the event loop deeply
  • Practice explaining your code out loud. If you can't explain it, you don't understand it
  • Solve at least 100 LeetCode problems focusing on arrays, trees, and graphs
  • Read about system design on high-level engineering blogs (Netflix Tech, Uber Engineering)

What Production Engineering Taught Me

Working on systems that serve real users at scale is fundamentally different from side projects. Things I learned only by working in production:

  • Monitoring and observability matter more than clever code. You need to know when things break before users complain
  • Database queries that work fine on 1,000 rows destroy production with 50 million rows
  • Code review isn't about catching bugs — it's about spreading knowledge across the team
  • The most valuable skill in a team is clear written communication, not raw coding ability
  • Simple code that everyone understands is worth far more than clever code that only you understand

What I'd Tell My Earlier Self

Stop waiting until you feel ready. Build more, finish more. Publish your code even when it's not perfect — especially when it's not perfect. Read source code from libraries you use. Contribute to open source, even documentation fixes count. Find communities online, they exist even when they don't exist physically near you.

Kashmir gave me patience. Mountains teach you that most worthwhile things take longer than you expect. Software engineering is the same — the journey from "I've heard of JavaScript" to shipping production code that serves millions of users is measured in years, not months. But it's absolutely worth it.
author: Owais Rafiq
